speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in line with the implementation of the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests, what initiatives are being planned to support small and medium enterprises in offering flexible work arrangements to their employees and enhance workplace productivity.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what likely impact will the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests have on senior PMETs aged 45 and above; (b) which sectors may be more impacted by the implementation of the guidelines; and (c) what is the positive impact on the Singapore economy in adopting the guidelines.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in view that all employers in Singapore must fairly consider requests for flexible work arrangements from 1 December 2024 under the new Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests (a) whether the Ministry can clarify what constitutes a "fair consideration"; and (b) how are employers held accountable for their decisions to accept or reject such requests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how has the Ministry ensured that employers are prepared to implement the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests, particularly regarding timelines and considerations for rejecting requests; (b) whether the Ministry can elaborate on the support and resources available, including any training initiatives, to assist businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises, in adapting to these new guidelines; and (c) how can we mitigate against employers turning towards outsourcing of work to overseas workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Minister for Manpower with the introduction of the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement (FWAs) Requests from December 2024 (a) whether there is any target or expected percentage of (i) firms that offer and (ii) employees that are covered by, formal FWAs; and (b) whether there are any legal ramifications for firms that do not adequately implement the guidelines.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower following the acceptance of the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests by the Government (a) what supportive measures will the Ministry be introducing to assist more companies during their transition in adopting these guidelines; and (b) whether there will be more resources made available to strengthen trust and harmonious workplace culture, including more avenues for mediation and dispute resolutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: My response will also cover today's Questions for Written Answer Parliamentary Question No 53 by Mr Yip Hon Weng, as well as four Questions for Written Answer by Mr Sharael Taha and Dr Wan Rizal scheduled for the Sitting on or after 8 May 2024.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In the past few years, many Members in this House and the Labour Movement have called the Government to do more to encourage FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: One in four Singaporeans will be above 65 years old by 2030.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: More of us will have to juggle caregiving responsibilities while working.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There will also be more seniors who want to continue working, but in a more flexible manner.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: FWAs are, therefore, another important initiative to help us optimise our local workforce potential in the long term.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers who implement FWAs well will also benefit, as they will be able to hire from a larger local manpower pool.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Hence, we formed a Tripartite Workgroup last year to develop a set of tripartite guidelines on FWA requests.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Workgroup consulted extensively with employees, the unions, employers and human resource (HR) professionals.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are a myriad and spectrum of businesses, service types and sector-specific needs which vary widely and serve different segments of the economy, including essential services.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For FWAs to be successful, it must make businesses sustainable for the employers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It does not make sense to require businesses to offer FWAs even when it negatively impacts business and affects employment prospects for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers should, therefore, continue to have the prerogative to determine work arrangements that work for the team, the business and the clients.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The aim is to establish the right norms, and enable employees and employers to have constructive discussions, so that both sides can work out FWAs that are mutually beneficial.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers must therefore consider FWAs based on business grounds, such as job requirements and impact to business productivity.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Tripartite partners agree that this is a reasonable and practical approach which balances the needs of both employees and employers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In the same spirit, the Workgroup felt that employers should be given sufficient time to discuss with employees their FWA requests and also consider how they can adjust workplace practices to accommodate FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Otherwise, employers may decide to reject the request outright.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Workgroup landed on two months which is similar to other jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employees who feel that the employers have not considered the FWA request based on proper process should first discuss and try to resolve disagreements internally through their company's grievance handling process.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Unionised employees can also seek advice from their respective unions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Thereafter, if the dispute is still not resolved, they may seek help from the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: TAFEP would take up an educational approach and engage the employers to help them comply with the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers who are recalcitrant may be issued a warning by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and be asked to attend mandatory HR training.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Several Members have asked about the impact of the guidelines on employers in different sectors and how we can help employers comply.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I must emphasise that FWAs do not equate to work-from-home only.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There is a variety of FWAs that employers can adopt depending on the industry context and the specific job role, while still maintaining productivity and ensuring that business needs are met.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For instance, those in sectors and jobs where the work must be done on-site may not be able to work from home, but employers can still explore options, such as flexi-time and flexi-load.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To be clear, the formal process for requesting FWAs, as recommended in the guidelines, will be useful mainly for organisations that do not have any process yet for their employees to request for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Where there is an existing process, whether formal or informal, and it is working well for both employers and employees, the employer should use the process stipulated by the company to request for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: What is most important is for the employees and employers to be able to discuss and land on arrangements that address their respective needs and constraints and maintain harmonious working relationships.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To help employers, TAFEP and the Institute for HR Professionals (IHRP) will be rolling out a range of resources this year.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Besides self-help resources, such as case studies, templates and e-learning modules, which are already available on TAFEP's website, TAFEP will be conducting monthly briefings for employers starting from May.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The first few runs have already been fully subscribed.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: TAFEP will provide more guidance to help employers understand the types of FWAs they can offer to employees with different needs, such as senior employees who may prefer flexi-load or mobility-challenged workers who may need telecommuting arrangements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The resources and briefings will guide employers on how to comply with the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But, more importantly, how to implement FWAs well, such that it supports business needs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers can also tap on grants, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant, to offset the cost of adopting FWAs, such as consultancy services, to redesign jobs or business processes and upgrade the IT system to support FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) may require more targeted support.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: TAFEP and IHRP will work closely with the Association for Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME) and the SME Centres, to organise briefings and training workshops to help SMEs in FWA implementation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Members have also asked about the potential impact of the guidelines on Singaporeans' employment prospects, be it through increased outsourcing to remote workers elsewhere or greater reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With or without these guidelines, remote work and outsourcing are already global trends, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Whether the trend will continue depends on whether employers feel that it makes business sense and employers will need to weigh the pros and cons.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Similarly, even if the foreigners are not working in Singapore, they will still be competing with us when working in companies overseas.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: What is more important is for our workers to continually upskill, sharpen our competitive edge and stay productive.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will, then, be able to compete effectively for jobs, not just in Singapore, but globally.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: FWAs are an increasingly important tool for employers to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employees ought to use FWAs responsibly, even as their employers develop HR capabilities and processes to implement FWAs well and productively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister of State, how will the Ministry facilitate and ensure HR professionals are equipped with the right framework and tools in implementing FWAs effectively in the workplace?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: HR professionals, indeed, are a key node in the successful implementation of FWAs and, hence, the Tripartite Work Group involved IHRP in the consultation and also drafting of the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In our various consultations leading up to the development of the guidelines, HR professionals were involved in various sessions to give us inputs on what sort of help and resources they might need.
Yesterday, I attended an engagement session with HR professionals facilitated by IHRP to share the tools, the courses and the resources available for HR professionals to tap on.

We welcome HR professionals to continue to give feedback to the Tripartite Workgroup and to IHRP as well as TAFEP on what are the other resources and help that HR professionals might need for them to do their job well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, would MOM agree that this should be left to employers and employees to negotiate and settle?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the worker is valued by the company, surely, the company would accede to that request.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why is there this need to have guidelines to make it mandatory for companies to consider such requests from employees?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The feedback I have is that many companies have told me that this is making it more onerous for a large company with many staff and for their HR team to have to deal with so many requests, especially for the staff that they feel that are on the borderline, that they may not want to keep.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, are we pushing the companies to say, "Let us get rid of the less performing staff?" At the end of the day, my concern is whether this will make Singapore a less attractive place for companies to come to invest in, if they feel that the manpower policies are too onerous on the companies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Prior to the guidelines, there had already been a lot of feedback from both employers and employees about expectations and requests on FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These guidelines are meant to help employers manage also the expectations of their employees.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We know that, coming out of COVID-19, there are some employees continually asking their employers and their supervisors, why can they not continue to work from home?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And some of the employers find it quite troubling and difficult to manage expectations of the employees.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: At the same time, we also hear anecdotal feedback from some employees that their employers are not receptive at all and not even responding to their request for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Just for your information, there are also many calls from the Members of the House, some of you might remember, for legislation, for the right to request and which we have seen in quite a few other countries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Instead of going the way of legislation, the tripartite partners, after a lot of consultation with various groups, felt that legislation would not be helpful.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We hope that employers and employees will make win-win outcomes out of these guidelines.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Speaker, just two supplementary questions for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is that I understand that based on the guidelines, cost, productivity and feasibility concerns are possible grounds for rejection of FWA requests.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I am also concerned that this could give employers a lot of leeway to actually not consider the FWA requests, where these are actually possible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, on the part of the employees, should there be concerns that their FWA requests are not adequately considered, beyond mediation and follow-up discussions with management, what are some of their recourse?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second part is I also understand that the Civil Service will be taking up these guidelines, so, just to understand what sort of percentage of civil servants will be able to access some form of formal FWAs after this is adopted?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employees who feel that their employers have not considered their requests properly, not based on business grounds but perhaps personal bias, can approach the union members or the union leaders if they are unionised companies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: TAFEP will be very happy to walk through with the employers on their responsibilities under the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Just like the private sector, we have a very big Civil Service and there are different job roles, different working environments.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We similarly need to give flexibility for the supervisors, managers to discuss with the staff on what sort of FWAs would work, not just for that one person asking for the FWA, but also how it affects the rest of the co-workers, and the services and the output that need to be delivered as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, again, refusing that their request for FWAs on unreasonable grounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, if the penalties are similar to the other tripartite guidelines, which is the curtailment of work pass privileges, for companies who do not employ foreigners, what then are the penalties for them?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore has a very tight labour market and there is always a shortage of skilled workers and talent.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: When we spoke to our counterparts overseas, countries that are in a very advanced stage of implementing FWAs and even with legislation, our key takeaway was that if the labour market is tight, employers who want to be able to attract and retain staff, they will actually be flexible themselves, even without the legislation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, employers, HR, people out there, by now, they already know the value of FWAs, how it is helping them as well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Like many, I welcome FWAs, especially from the mental health perspective.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I do have concerns from employees who want to step forward.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I think they are fearing this idea of being discriminated against.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They fear that their personal issues may be resurfaced now and then, it will be used against them in terms of career progression and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What considerations would the Ministry take to provide clear assurances to such employees?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For workers who have certain health conditions, whether it is mental or other sorts of health issues, employers have to assess, evaluate their performance and pay them fairly based on the work that is done by them and not discriminate them based on conditions such as health that do not affect their performance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I have got two supplementary questions for the Minister of State.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The first one is, as the Minister of State has pointed out, the labour market is tight and corporates are also finding ways to adjust with how to cope with the labour supply.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Does Minister of State think that we will likely see an increase of offshoring of jobs as a result of this implementation of the guidelines?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The second supplementary question is with regard to the union.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, we are seeing an increasing trend of having more professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) as your union members as well.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For Singaporeans to stay competitive and be desirable in terms of jobs and employability, we need to have the relevant skills, we need to be productive, we need to have the competitive edge.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Offshoring, outsourcing, post-COVID, companies that found that remote work worked well for the business, they would have continued to do so, even without these guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In fact, businesses are driven by their own bottom lines, what works well in terms of them being able to access talent and also cost.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We should not pretend that without FWAs, there will be less offshoring.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I would also point out that elsewhere, in the United States, for example, we are also seeing some tech companies putting out statements that remote work does not work for them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There seems to be some suggestion that for certain sectors and for certain types of work, physical, on-site presence, teamwork, all these are still very key.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Some of the companies that we have engaged in Singapore have shared similar feedback.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And for those, offshoring may not be a natural choice and certainly, would not be affected by these guidelines.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As for middle-aged workers, PMETs, our focus must be on preparing them well for jobs for life, upskilling them, making sure there are enough job opportunities in various sectors so that whether you are PMET or non-PMET, you will continue to enjoy good career prospects.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Career health is another strategy that we are working on to help middle-aged workers stay employable.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are many schemes at the Government level to support the middle-aged workers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I hope Members will support us in these initiatives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, I would like to ask the Minister of State how will FWAs interface with the Progressive Wage Model (PWM)?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For flexi-load, for example, where a worker in one of these sectors requests to work less days, that may bring his gross wage to below the PWM prescribed wage floor.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the employer then be required to immediately reject this, so that he remains compliant with the PWM?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I would say that employers have to pay competitively in order to be able to attract good people to join them and to retain them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Speaker, I thank the Member of Parliament for his supplementary question.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has taken into account the underlying basis of tripartism and how we work with all of our tripartite partners to come to a very nuanced approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I would seek and appeal to the understanding, the support and also the patience of all of us together as one united society, to come together to make this work for the betterment of all of our future generations of workers.
